Muscle memory discovery ends 'use it or lose it' dogma

Well the headline is wrong. This has nothing to do with muscle memory, which is a synaptic effect mostly manifest in the cerebellum. It has to do with the nature of muscle atrophy and reversal thereof due to retention of myonuclei. It was previously believed that muscle mass/volume directly drove the number of myonuclei, but improved research shows that significant muscle mass growth adds myonuclei (as expected and previously known), but that the tissue lost in atrophy does not include significant amounts of myonuclei (at least compared to the amounts previously thought). The end result is that it's much easier to add back muscle mass in muscles that a subject had previously built up then lost due to atrophy. Presumably because it's easier to add actin/myosin (muscle fiber) and supporting vascular structures than it is to add myonuclei.

But this has nothing to do with optimized synaptic pathways supporting complex compound behaviors like walking, swimming, bike riding, playing a musical instrument, etc, all manifestations of muscle memory.
Hence why exposing children to all types of activities and sports at an early age has lasting affect later in life.
